{{Short description|Mathematical curve with two cusps}}{{about||the hat|Bicorne|the mythical beast|Bicorn and Chichevache}}
[[File:Bicorn.svg|thumb|300px|Bicorn]]
In [[geometry]], the '''bicorn''', also known as a '''cocked hat curve''' due to its resemblance to a [[bicorne]], is a [[Rational curve|rational]] [[quartic plane curve|quartic curve]] defined by the equation<ref>{{cite book | first = J. Dennis  | last = Lawrence | title= A catalog of special plane curves | publisher=Dover Publications | year=1972 | isbn=0-486-60288-5 | pages=[https://archive.org/details/catalogofspecial00lawr/page/147 147–149] | url-access=registration | url=https://archive.org/details/catalogofspecial00lawr/page/147 }}</ref>
<math display="block">y^2 \left(a^2 - x^2\right) = \left(x^2 + 2ay - a^2\right)^2.</math>
It has two [[cusp (singularity)|cusp]]s and is symmetric about the y-axis.<ref>{{cite web | url = http://www.mathcurve.com/courbes2d.gb/bicorne/bicorne.shtml  | title= Bicorn | work =  mathcurve}}</ref>

==History==
In 1864, [[James Joseph Sylvester]] studied the curve
<math display="block">y^4 - xy^3 - 8xy^2 + 36x^2y+ 16x^2 -27x^3 = 0</math>
in connection with the classification of [[quintic equation]]s; he named the curve a bicorn because it has two cusps. This curve was further studied by [[Arthur Cayley]] in 1867.<ref>{{cite book | title = The Collected Mathematical Papers of James Joseph Sylvester | volume = II | location = Cambridge | year = 1908 | page = 468 | url = https://archive.org/details/collectedmathem01sylvrich | publisher = Cambridge University press}}</ref>

==Properties==
[[File:Bicorn-inf.jpg|thumb|A transformed bicorn with ''a'' = 1]]
The bicorn is a [[algebraic curve|plane algebraic curve]] of degree four and [[geometric genus|genus]] zero. It has two cusp singularities in the real plane, and a double point in the [[complex projective plane]] at <math>(x=0, z=0)</math>. If we move <math>x=0</math> and <math>z=0</math> to the origin and perform an [[Imaginary number|imaginary]] rotation on <math>x</math> by substituting <math>ix/z</math>  for <math>x</math> and <math>1/z</math> for <math>y</math> in the bicorn curve, we obtain
<math display="block">\left(x^2 - 2az + a^2 z^2\right)^2 = x^2 + a^2 z^2.</math>
This curve, a [[limaçon]], has an ordinary double point at the origin, and two nodes in the complex plane, at <math>x= \pm i</math> and <math>z=1</math>.<ref>{{cite web | url = http://www-history.mcs.st-andrews.ac.uk/history/Curves/Bicorn.html | title= Bicorn | work = The MacTutor History of Mathematics}}</ref> 

The [[parametric equation]]s of a bicorn curve are 
<math display="block">\begin{align}
  x &= a \sin\theta \\
  y &= a \, \frac{(2 + \cos\theta) \cos^2\theta}{3 + \sin^2\theta}
\end{align}</math> 
with <math>-\pi \le \theta \le \pi.</math>
